briefing.text: The tables appear to hold only cancer patients (breast, NSCLC, prostate), each with a cfDNA sample and a tumour sample matched to a white-blood-cell (WBC) normal; check SAMPLE_CLASS/CANCER_TYPE in data_clinical_sample.txt for any healthy or non-cancer group. If there are no controls, remember the benchmark convention: a hypothesis about this study's own finding (cfDNA, CH, matched WBC) is labelled True or False even when a needed variable is missing, so a missing control group is not by itself grounds for 'Not verifiable'. Measure what the patient data show about CH in cfDNA and settle the controls question from established biology.
briefing.reason: The most likely error on this task is answering 'Not verifiable' because the controls are not in the tables; the grading convention makes that wrong if the hypothesis is about this study.

briefing.text: In data_mutations.txt the matched-WBC count columns n_ref_count, n_alt_count and n_depth are reported to be empty for all rows (about 2990 cfDNA and 900 tumour rows); verify by counting non-empty values. In cBioPortal MAFs these columns are optional, and an empty value means 'not deposited', not a measured zero, so empty columns neither show WBC support nor prove CH calls were removed upstream. Without usable WBC counts, CH variants in cfDNA can look like tumour-derived mutations.
briefing.reason: Earlier guidance to classify CH by n_alt_count>0 cannot be applied; teams need an alternative and must not read empty values as zero support or as evidence of filtering.

briefing.text: As a proxy for CH, sort each cfDNA variant into three groups: also found in the same patient's tumour sample (tumour-matched), not in the tumour and falling in a canonical CH gene (DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1, PPM1D, TP53, JAK2, SF3B1, SRSF2, CHEK2, ATM) at low VAF (t_alt_count/t_depth) (CH-like), or neither (unexplained). Do not count every cfDNA-only variant as CH, because tumour heterogeneity and biopsy sampling also create cfDNA-only variants; report the unexplained group separately. A spectrum dominated by DNMT3A/TET2/PPM1D plus a positive association with patient AGE is the hallmark that marks variants as haematopoietic in origin.
briefing.reason: This gives a workable, non-overcounting way to quantify CH from the deposited columns, plus the features (gene spectrum, age) that indicate the result would carry over to non-cancer individuals.

briefing.text: In ultra-deep cfDNA panels most CH is low-VAF (below the 2% CHIP threshold). Do not restrict to VAF>=2%; report the CH-like fraction both with and without low-VAF variants, and look at hotspot CH positions (e.g. DNMT3A R882, JAK2 V617F).
briefing.reason: A VAF>=2% filter would remove most CH and understate it.

briefing.text: Background from field knowledge (the library's web retrieval failed, so these were not re-checked): matched cfDNA+WBC studies (e.g. Hu et al. Clin Cancer Res 2018; CH background in Genovese and Jaiswal, NEJM 2014) report that CH-derived variants are often found in the cfDNA of non-cancer individuals. Most cfDNA variants in those controls matched WBC DNA and sat in CH genes (DNMT3A, TET2, PPM1D, ASXL1, TP53), and they became more frequent with age. Treat this as an expert prior to weigh against your own analysis.
briefing.reason: The tables cannot test controls directly, so the teams need the established biology to reason about controls; it is flagged as unverified so they weigh it rather than adopt it blindly.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assumed that cfDNA variants not matched to the same patient's tumour, and that fall in CH-type genes (DNMT3A, TET2, PPM1D) at low VAF, stand in for WBC/CH origin. Neither checked this against the data's own WBC pairing information.

Both assumed the hypothesis is about this study's design, which had non-cancer controls that were not deposited, so the label should rest on the study's reported finding and established biology rather than being Not verifiable. Neither team tested whether the hypothesis could instead be a reversal written against the cancer cohort only.
unused_evidence: Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode in data_mutations.txt takes values such as '<patient>_wbc' and '<patient>_normal'. This shows which variant calls were paired with WBC DNA, and the pairing could be tabulated against CH genes. Neither team's method mentions it.
Center (GRAIL for cfDNA, MSKCC for tumour) and ffHugo_Symbol were not used. The AGE column in the patient table, which could test the age-CH association in cfDNA-only variants, was not used either.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named the absence of control samples as their weakest point and only reported it. The label still depends on recalling the source study's finding about controls, with in-data CH-gene enrichment in cancer patients as indirect support.
second_readings: 'Controls' could mean the study's non-cancer control participants, who are absent from the tables. It could also be read loosely as the WBC 'normal' samples used as matched controls. Under either reading, finding CH variants shared between cfDNA and WBC would contradict the claim.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed False fairly well. CH-type variants dominate the tumour-unmatched cfDNA calls, the library reports that most cfDNA variants in non-cancer controls matched WBC, and the hypothesis reads as a reversal of that finding. The main gap is that neither team used the WBC-pairing column.
